::: {.key-points}
**Key points**

- The **Scottish Observatory for Atmospheric Research (SOAR)**, near Invergowrie
  west of Dundee, is the UK's first 100-metre tower built for atmospheric science.
  The rest of the UK network uses telecommunications towers.
- GEMMA funded instruments at the tower, including one measuring more than 40
  halogenated greenhouse gases.
- With Invergowrie data, the Met Office's emissions model maps Scotland's methane
  and nitrous oxide emissions in far more detail than before, with **population
  centres around Edinburgh and Glasgow now visible**.
- This gives the Scottish Government a growing, independent check on Scotland's
  own emissions figures.
:::

## Why this matters

Scotland has a legal target to reach net zero by 2045, tracked through five-year
carbon budgets. Progress is measured using Scotland's share of the UK greenhouse
gas inventory, which is calculated from statistics such as livestock numbers, fuel
use and landfill records. Measuring the gases in the atmosphere gives an
independent check on those figures.

The UK Deriving Emissions linked to Climate Change (DECC) network does this for the
UK, but most of its stations are in England or at Mace Head in Ireland. Air from
Scotland reaches them only after travelling a long way, so the network could only
estimate Scotland's emissions across a few large regions.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![The 100-metre SOAR tower at Balruddery, near Invergowrie, with the Firth of Tay and Dundee behind. Photo: The James Hutton Institute.](/research-highlights/figures/invergowrie-fig1.jpg){fig-alt="Aerial photograph of a tall, thin lattice mast rising from a small cabin beside a belt of woodland, surrounded by farmland, with the Firth of Tay and the Tay road bridge in the distance."}
:::


## What GEMMA did

SOAR stands on the James Hutton Institute's Balruddery research farm near
Invergowrie. It is jointly owned by the James Hutton Institute and the University
of Edinburgh, and samples air at 50 and 100 metres. Because the prevailing winds
are westerly, the air it samples has crossed much of Scotland, including the
central belt.

```{=typst}

// lands at the top of the right-hand column, below the key points.
#place(top, float: true, clearance: 0.8em, block[
  #align(center)[#image("figures/invergowrie-fig1.jpg", width: 100%)]
  #v(0.15em)
  #text(size: 0.82em, fill: rgb("#26557a"))[*Figure 1:* The 100-metre SOAR tower at Balruddery, near Invergowrie, with the Firth of Tay and Dundee behind. Photo: The James Hutton Institute.]
])
```

GEMMA funded the deployment of some of the new SOAR instruments, principally a **Medusa** gas chromatograph-mass
spectrometer that measures more than 40 halogenated gases, such as the
hydrofluorocarbons used in refrigeration and air conditioning. Measurements of
methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) at the site began in May 2025.

The Met Office then ran its Inversion Technique for Emissions Modelling (InTEM),
which works backwards from measured concentrations and weather patterns to
estimate where gases were emitted, for 2024 and 2025 with and without the
Invergowrie data.

Triangles mark measurement sites.](/research-highlights/figures/invergowrie-fig2.png){fig-alt="Two maps of Scotland coloured by estimated methane emissions in kilograms per square kilometre per year. The left map shows broad, uniform blocks across central and southern Scotland. The right map, which uses Invergowrie data, shows a smaller grid with markedly higher emissions concentrated in the central belt between Edinburgh and Glasgow. A triangle marks the Invergowrie site on the Firth of Tay."}

- Methane emissions in the central belt, previously spread across large regions,
  now stand out. Nitrous oxide maps show the same gain in detail.
- The uncertainty in monthly emissions estimates for both gases fell once
  Invergowrie data were added.
- These results use only seven and a half months of measurements. Estimates will
  improve as the record grows.

## What this means for policy

The UK's atmospheric monitoring network can now look at emissions within
Scotland in much finer detail. As the record builds, this will give the Scottish
Government independent evidence on whether reported emissions, and their trends,
match the atmosphere: for methane and nitrous oxide now, and for halogenated gases
once the Medusa data have been analysed.

## What comes next

- Continue measurements, so that each additional year tightens estimates of
  Scotland's emissions.
- Add Invergowrie's hydrogen data to GEMMA's hydrogen analysis.
- Estimate Scotland's halogenated gas emissions from the Medusa data.
